keywords.def: A plant whose fruit, seeds, roots, tubers, bulbs, stems, leaves or flowers are eaten as food, usually fresh.

en.text: Vegetables are plants whose fruit, seeds, roots, tubers, bulbs, stems, leaves or flowers are eaten; they supply vitamins, minerals and, in legumes, protein. They are classified by edible part, temperature requirement or life cycle. Ethiopia's diverse climates, land, water and labour make many vegetables possible. Temperature, light, water, humidity, soil and altitude affect production, and systems range from gathering wild vegetables to commercial production.

screens.title: Warm up: which part do we eat?
Unit summary
paras: Vegetables: plants whose fruit, seeds, roots, tubers, bulbs, stems, leaves or flowers are eaten.
They are rich in vitamins and minerals; legumes add plant protein.
Classified by edible part, temperature requirement or life cycle.
Ethiopia has diverse climates, vast land and water, and a large work force.
Temperature, light, water, humidity, soil and altitude affect production.
Systems range from gathering wild vegetables to commercial production.
screens.note: The book's summary says vegetables exclude fruits and seeds. That contradicts p.2 and its own examples (tomato, beans). Use the p.2 definition.

screens.title: Key word
defs: A plant whose fruit, seeds, roots, tubers, bulbs, stems, leaves or flowers are eaten as food, usually fresh.

screens.text: Which three bases does the book use to classify vegetables?
opts: Edible part, temperature requirement, life cycle
Seed size, leaf colour, root depth
screens.ans: Edible part, temperature requirement, life cycle
screens.clue: Look back at the three ideas of 1.3.

screens.text: Tomato and green beans are not vegetables, because they are a fruit and a seed.
screens.why: p.2 defines vegetables to include fruit and seeds; tomato and green beans are among the book's main vegetables.

screens.text: Which are environmental factors that affect vegetable production?
screens.why: Market price matters for profit but is not an environmental factor.

screens.text: Which system supplies most vegetables to urban populations?
A Debre Birhan farmer (about 2,800 m) chooses between cabbage and watermelon for the Addis market. Which is the better choice?
opts: Cabbage: a hardy cool-season crop suits the cool highland
Watermelon: very tender crops like cold
screens.ans: Cabbage: a hardy cool-season crop suits the cool highland
screens.why: High altitude means low temperature; hardy cool-season cabbage fits, while very tender watermelon needs warmth.
screens.clue: Combine altitude with each crop's temperature group.
